Morocco’s exceptional heat wave is expected to ease gradually over the coming days, although temperatures could rise again toward the end of the week and into early next week, the country’s weather service said Wednesday.
The General Directorate of Meteorology attributed the unusually hot conditions at the beginning of September to the influence of a Saharan thermal low extending toward central and northern Morocco, combined with a continued flow of very hot and dry continental tropical air masses from the Sahara.
The conditions have strengthened the prevalence of easterly winds, locally known as “Chergui,” across inland areas.
Monthly temperature records were recorded in several areas, particularly on Sept. 3. Temperatures reached 47.1 degrees Celsius in Sidi Slimane, 45.1 C in Kenitra and 44.3 C in Sale, according to data provided by the meteorological service.
Despite the widespread heat, localized thunderstorms developed in the Atlas Mountains, at times accompanied by hail and strong winds.
Gradual decline expected
Temperatures are expected to decline gradually over the next two days from the exceptional levels recorded late last week and at the beginning of this week, said El Hussein Youabed, a communications official with the General Directorate of Meteorology.
Temperatures are expected to return gradually toward levels closer to seasonal averages, although the decline will not necessarily mark the end of unsettled weather, Youabed said.
Some areas, particularly the Atlas Mountains, the southeastern region and parts of southern Morocco, are expected to remain vulnerable to unstable clouds and localized thunderstorms, especially during the afternoon.
Youabed cautioned that the easing temperatures do not necessarily mean the end of hot weather.
Another rise in temperatures remains possible toward the end of this week and early next week, particularly in inland areas, the southeast, Souss and desert regions, he said.
September is a transitional month between summer and the beginning of autumn, Youabed said, making fluctuations in temperatures and alternating periods of heat and more moderate weather normal for the time of year.
The transition can also bring periods of atmospheric instability, including localized thunderstorms, he said.
Heat and thunderstorms under orange alert
The meteorological service issued a new orange-level weather warning Wednesday, covering two weather phenomena expected to occur simultaneously.
The first involves continued hot weather in several southern and southeastern provinces. Temperatures were forecast to reach between 42 C and 45 C in Tata, Smara, Laayoune, Assa-Zag, Boujdour, Oued Ed-Dahab and Aousserd.
Temperatures of between 38 C and 42 C were expected in Guelmim, Taroudant, Tan-Tan and Tarfaya.
The second warning concerns thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong wind gusts. Rainfall totals of between 25 and 35 millimeters were forecast between 1 p.m. and 11 p.m. Wednesday in Ifrane, Ouarzazate, Azilal, Beni Mellal, Fquih Ben Salah, Boulemane, Midelt and Khenifra.
The weather pattern reflects the transitional nature of September, with periods of intense heat expected to alternate with localized thunderstorms and other episodes of unsettled weather in the days ahead.

title: ‘Why was Mum in clothes you could wear in the winter?’: family seeks answers after care home heatstroke death - The Guardian

Anita Bazell had never coped with the heat very well, her family said. So they were worried about her when temperatures across the UK soared to record highs of 35C (95F) in May, and then again in June.
She was living in a nursing home in Southampton near her family, who had struggled to care for her at home due to her declining mobility. Although there were air conditioning units in the communal rooms, there was not one in Anita’s room, which was on the third floor.
“I used to see her every weekend. Heat rises and she was on the top floor, and the windows were open as far as the restrictors would let them go,” said her son, Steve Bazell. “It was hot in there. It was so hot you couldn’t sleep at night around here back then.”
The first phone call came on 25 June – Steve was told his mother was feeling unwell and she was being taken to bed. “I remember it because it was the hottest day on record [for June] that day,” Steve said. It was actually the second of three days that week when the temperature record for June was broken.
The next phone call, just after 9am the following day, was a shock. Paramedics called to say his mother had been found unresponsive and was being taken to Southampton general hospital. The family were urged to get there as soon as possible – medics were not sure she would make it to the hospital.
When they arrived, Anita’s face looked drooped on one side and they thought she had suffered a stroke. Doctors were putting towels soaked in ice water on her, replacing them every few minutes. The family were soon told she had been diagnosed with heatstroke, which had caused a bleed on the brain.
When she arrived in hospital, she had a body temperature of 41.2C – anything above 40C is considered a medical emergency.
“You could see her improving as she was getting cooler but she was still unresponsive,” he said. “We had mixed reactions. I mean, my mum was 88, but she was mentally fine. We couldn’t understand how this had happened – did they check on her?”
Anita was hospitalised on 26 June, which was then the hottest June day on record in the UK with 38C recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk, breaking the previous record of 35.6 degrees set in Southampton 50 years earlier. It was the fifth hottest day in the UK ever.
Steve was told Anita was one of at least seven elderly people taken to Southampton general hospital with heatstroke that day, and some did not make it there before they died.
The day before Anita’s admission, University hospital Southampton NHS foundation trust had declared a critical incident due to the extreme heat, which forced some operations and appointments to be cancelled.
David Higgs, the hospital’s deputy chief medical officer, later said Southampton general came “very close to collapse” during the June heatwave, which was “in many ways almost worse than Covid”.
“There was a huge amount of attendances in our emergency department. Primary care was overflooded. The ambulance service pretty much collapsed,” he told the city’s health and wellbeing board.
Steve said the hospital set up a special “cooling” ward specifically to deal with the influx of patients with heatstroke. Staff ran out of towels to soak in ice water to cool patients down, and resorted to cutting up bed sheets. “I remember I went upstairs to get more towels and help,” said Steve. “The hospital was really good. But they were stretched.”
Anita’s condition improved once her body temperature reduced, but ultimately there was nothing that could be done to save her. Over the next few days, Steve said her eyes would follow family members as they moved around her, and she could gently squeeze a hand when asked, but never regained full consciousness.
Steve and his sister took it in turns maintaining a bedside vigil every day until at least 10pm at night. He said they were a small but close family, and his mother devoted much of her life to supporting them.
As the siblings were growing up, Anita worked as a dinner lady and in their school library, volunteered as a Cub scout leader and supported them in their hobbies of motorbike racing and horse riding. She was married to her late husband, Les, for more than 50 years.
Anita died on 6 July with heatstroke recorded as her cause of death.
She is one of thousands of people believed to have died a heat-related death during the extreme hot weather this year. There were an estimated 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during the May and June heatwaves, nearly double the 1,504 excess deaths recorded for the entire summer of 2025.
With four more heatwaves recorded across July and August, heat-related deaths this summer are expected to be the highest on record.
On 24 June, the Met Office issued a rare red heat weather warning due to the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and predicted increased mortality and hospital admissions due to heat-related illness.
Some deaths may be linked to exertional heatstroke, caused by heavy physical exercise. Sophie Goodyer-Bird, a 35-year-old woman from Birmingham, died of heatstroke after climbing Yr Wyddfa – also known as Snowdon – on 10 July.
But most of the fatalities will be among the elderly population, although heatstroke is rarely recorded on death certificates as extreme heat often acts as an indirect trigger, placing severe strain on pre-existing health conditions that can be fatal.
Care homes for elderly people are on the frontline of dealing with this – during the July 2022 heatwave, nursing home deaths increased by 34.1% and residential care home deaths increased by 13.0%.
This year, many care homes reported using fans, air conditioners, paddling pools, ice lollies and cold fruit to keep residents cool. But research has found many are still underprepared for severe heat caused by the climate crisis.
The Care Quality Commission is investigating a care home in Watford after four residents were taken to hospital during the May heatwave, with one dying and the others “coming to harm”. An inspection report said there were concerns residents were left “at risk of dehydration”.
Anita’s family has written to her nursing home – which they have chosen not to name until investigations are complete – as they have concerns about the care she received in the hours before she collapsed.
After her death they were given the clothes she was wearing when she was brought into hospital, which Steve described as “a short-sleeve woolly jumper and wool trousers”. He said: “Why was Mum in clothes you could wear in the winter? And how long had she been wearing them for?”
Steve said he wanted to raise awareness of the risks of heatstroke, particularly among elderly people in care homes, with more extreme heat on its way next year.
“They’re already saying it’s going to be hotter next year,” he said. “What my mum went through, what we went through as a family, it’s really not a very pleasant experience. I’m not saying it wouldn’t have happened anyway, but I do want to know if anything could have been done differently.”

title: Ray LaMontagne Collapsed Onstage in Nashville and Heat Illness Does Not Require an Outdoor Heat Warning - Medical Daily

full_text:
Singer-songwriter Ray LaMontagne collapsed during a concert at Nashville's Ryman Auditorium on Sept. 5, and his management later said he was treated by local emergency medical services for heat-related dehydration. He recovered, performed as scheduled in Louisville the following night, and his team said he was doing well, according to wire coverage of the incident.
The detail worth pausing on is where it happened. This was an indoor concert hall in early September, not a stadium in July, and no extreme heat alert was in effect. Several attendees described the room as unusually warm.
That combination is more common than most people assume. Heat illness is often filed mentally under outdoor summer risk, tied to a forecast number and a public warning. In practice, packed indoor rooms, physical exertion, alcohol, and inadequate fluids can produce the same physiology without any of the external cues people rely on to take it seriously.
Sequence of Events Described at the Ryman
According to reporting from Consequence, LaMontagne, 53, sank to the stage during the later portion of his set while performing "Jolene," and people nearby moved in immediately to assist. He was helped offstage, and the concert ended early.
Earlier in the same set, he had stopped twice during another song after appearing to lose his place, apologized to the audience, and briefly left the stage before returning. In hindsight, those moments read as possible early signs rather than performance slips, though nothing has been publicly confirmed about his condition at the time.
His management said in a statement posted to his Instagram story that he was being treated for heat-related dehydration and was doing well. The show was the second of two nights at the venue on a tour in which he performs his 2004 debut album in full.
One caution belongs up front. That description came from the artist's representatives, not from a treating physician or hospital, and no clinical statement has been released. Heat-related dehydration is plausible given the circumstances, but a brief loss of consciousness onstage can have several causes.
Indoor Rooms Where Air Conditioning Is Not Enough
Large indoor venues fight a losing battle with their own audiences. Each person in a packed room produces body heat continuously, and a full house generates a substantial thermal load. Stage lighting adds more. Air conditioning sized for typical occupancy can fall behind on a warm evening when the room is full.
Performers face a version of this that the audience does not. Singing is physical work, and playing an instrument under stage lights while wearing performance clothing for 90 minutes is closer to moderate exercise than to sitting in a seat. Fluid losses accumulate quietly, and there is no natural pause to drink.
The underlying principle in the National Weather Service's heat safety materials is that risk tracks exposure and exertion rather than the presence of an alert. That guidance is aimed at outdoor conditions, but the logic transfers to a hot, crowded room where a performer is working hard for an hour and a half.
The scale of the annual burden is significant. A CDC fact sheet states that in an average year, heat causes 67,512 emergency department visits, 9,235 hospitalizations, and 702 deaths in the United States.
Warning Signs That Usually Arrive Before a Collapse
Dehydration and heat exhaustion rarely appear without warning. Common early signs include thirst, dry mouth, headache, dizziness or lightheadedness when standing, dark urine or infrequent urination, muscle cramps, nausea, unusual fatigue, and irritability. Heavy sweating with cool, clammy skin and a rapid but weak pulse points toward heat exhaustion.
Cognitive changes are the ones people around the person are best positioned to notice. Confusion, slurred speech, losing track of a task, or acting out of character can signal that the situation is progressing. Losing one's place mid-performance, mid-sentence, or mid-conversation is worth taking seriously in a hot room.
The response to suspected heat exhaustion is to move to a cooler place, sit or lie down, loosen clothing, apply cool, damp cloths, and sip water slowly. Symptoms that worsen after an hour, or vomiting that prevents drinking, warrant medical attention.
Heatstroke is a separate emergency requiring a call to 911. Its markers are a body temperature of 103 degrees or higher, hot skin that may be dry or damp, a fast and strong pulse, confusion, and loss of consciousness. A person with suspected heatstroke should not be given anything to drink. Anyone who faints should be evaluated, because a collapse can also reflect a cardiac rhythm problem, low blood sugar, a blood pressure drop or a medication effect.
Practical Guidance for Audiences, Performers and Venue Staff
Concertgoers can reduce their own risk with a few unremarkable habits. Drink water before and during a show rather than waiting for thirst, treat alcohol as a fluid loss rather than a fluid gain, and step into a lobby or outdoors if the room feels oppressive. Standing still in a crowd for long stretches also pools blood in the legs, which contributes to fainting independent of heat.
People at higher risk should plan a little more deliberately. That includes older adults, pregnant people, anyone with heart or kidney disease, and people taking diuretics, beta blockers, antipsychotics, stimulants or medications with anticholinergic effects. Nobody should stop a prescribed medication, but a pharmacist can explain how a given drug interacts with heat and hydration.
Performers, touring crews, and venue staff work in the highest exposure position in the building. Water available onstage, monitoring of room temperature during full house shows, and a clear internal threshold for pausing a performance are basic protections. The Ryman incident resolved well in part because people were close enough to reach him within seconds and emergency medical services were on site.
For audiences, the most useful takeaway is behavioral rather than medical. If someone nearby looks unwell in a hot, crowded room, flag venue staff rather than waiting to see whether it passes. Most of these episodes end the way this one appears to have ended, with rest, fluids, and a return to normal within hours.
Key Questions Answered
What happened at the Ryman Auditorium? LaMontagne collapsed onstage during his Sept. 5 concert while performing "Jolene." He was helped offstage, the show ended early, and his management said he was treated by local emergency medical services for heat-related dehydration.
Is he all right now? His team said he was doing well and he performed as scheduled at the Louisville Palace the following night.
Was the cause medically confirmed? No. The explanation came from the artist's representatives, not from a treating physician or hospital. No clinical statement has been released.
Can heat illness happen indoors? Yes. Crowded rooms, stage lighting, physical exertion, alcohol, and inadequate fluid intake can produce dehydration and heat exhaustion without any outdoor heat alert in effect.
What are the early warning signs? Thirst, headache, dizziness on standing, dark or infrequent urine, cramps, nausea, unusual fatigue, and heavy sweating with cool, clammy skin. Confusion or losing track of a task is a more serious signal.
When should someone call 911? For a body temperature of 103 degrees or higher, hot skin, a fast and strong pulse, confusion, or loss of consciousness. Do not give anything to drink to someone with suspected heatstroke.
Should a person who faints at a concert see a doctor? Yes. Fainting has several possible causes beyond heat, including cardiac rhythm problems, low blood sugar, and medication effects, and it merits evaluation even after a quick recovery.

SINGAPORE: The Category A certificate of entitlement (COE) premium hit an all-time high of S$133,009 in the Wednesday (Sept 9) tender exercise, even as the prices rose across all the other categories.
Meant for smaller, less powerful cars and electric vehicles (EVs), the latest Category A COE price was 3.5 per cent higher than the $128,501 posted at the previous tender, overtaking the $129,000 record set in July 2026.
The price for a Category B COE – used to register larger, more powerful cars and EVs – inched up 3.1 per cent from $131,001 to $135,001, the highest since November 2023 when it hit $135,336.
The higher COE premiums come after a three-week interval from the previous exercise, instead of the usual two weeks. Motor dealers said that the extra one week gives the trade more time to accumulate orders.
Open category (Category E) COE premium also rose 2.1 per cent from $135,000 to $137,890.
As these certificates are transferrable, motor traders often secure them for the flexibility to register cars without waiting for the next tender exercise.
The price of certificates for commercial vehicles (Category C) was 3.4 per cent higher than the previous $90,002, ending at $93,101.
The motorcycle (Category D) COE premium posted an 11.1 per cent hike from $11,301 to $12,556. This is the fifth consecutive round that the price of such certificates rose, edging closer to the $13,189 peak recorded in November 2022. - The Straits Times/ANN

Heavy rainfall over Delhi on 4 September caused waterlogging at Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport and disrupted flight operations, with more than 400 flights delayed and 11 flights diverted to nearby cities including Jaipur, Lucknow and Ahmedabad.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for heavy to very heavy rainfall over the capital, forecasting continued moderate to heavy showers accompanied by strong winds of 40-50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph. A sudden squall during the afternoon produced wind speeds of approximately 76 kmph, coinciding with heavy rain that sharply reduced visibility and worsened surface conditions at the airport.
Intense afternoon showers left the forecourts and key access areas of IGI Airport waterlogged, with passengers reportedly forced to wade through pooled water to reach departure and arrival zones. The disruption peaked between the mid-afternoon and early evening hours, with flight tracking data showing average delays of around 20 to 30 minutes, though some departures were pushed back by significantly longer margins. The intensity of the storm forced a cluster of arriving aircraft to abort landing attempts.
IGI Airport issued a passenger advisory warning of disruptions to flight operations. IndiGo, one of the largest carriers operating at the airport, issued a travel advisory urging passengers to monitor their flight status closely and arrive at the airport with additional time in hand, citing the risk of delays and diversions caused by the weather. Other major carriers also flagged possible disruptions in similar advisories.
Airport operators indicated that runway operations remained technically open throughout, but the surrounding infrastructure and access roads struggled to cope with the intensity of the rainfall, with waterlogging reported in low-lying underpasses along key routes to the airport. Passengers travelling from Noida, Ghaziabad and outer Gurugram were advised to build in additional buffer time for road transit, given the persistent congestion on approach roads.
The IMD has indicated that rainfall intensity over Delhi is likely to ease from 6 September onward, with forecasts pointing to a shift from heavy showers toward lighter, more scattered rain. However, with saturated ground conditions and lingering thunderstorms, the risk of short-notice disruptions was expected to remain elevated in the immediate aftermath.
The episode adds to a recurring pattern of monsoon-related disruption at IGI Airport in recent years, with previous drainage upgrades at the airport having repeatedly struggled to cope with sudden, high-volume rainfall events, particularly around Terminal 3's forecourt and approach roads.
